# How to Get Started with Midjourney: A Practical Guide for Everyday Creators

> **In short:** Midjourney turns text descriptions into images. Sign up at midjourney.com, choose a paid plan, type a prompt, and within a minute you'll get four image options. Here's every click, from sign-up to a finished picture on your computer.

You need a picture that doesn't exist yet — a birthday card, a blog header, a poster for your band's next gig. Midjourney is one of the most popular **AI image generators** (tools that create pictures from text descriptions), and it works well even if you can't draw. Here's how to actually use it.

## Before you start

You'll need:

- A computer or phone with a modern browser (Chrome, Safari, Firefox)
- An email address, Google account, or Discord account
- A payment method (credit card or PayPal)
- Around $10 USD for the cheapest plan — Midjourney no longer offers a reliable free tier

Midjourney runs at **midjourney.com** in your browser. There's also a Discord version, but the website is calmer for first-timers and easier to follow with screenshots.

## Step 1 — Create your account

Open **midjourney.com** in your browser. In the top-right corner, click **Sign In**. You'll see options to continue with **Google**, **Discord**, or **Email**. Pick whichever you already use — Google is fastest for most people. After you authorize the sign-in, Midjourney redirects you back to its home page.

💬 Example path: `midjourney.com → top-right Sign In → Continue with Google`

You'll know it worked when: you see your username or profile picture in the top-right corner of the page.

## Step 2 — Pick a subscription plan

Midjourney will prompt you to subscribe before you can generate anything. Look for a **Subscribe** or **Get Started** button — it's usually visible on the home page or in the left sidebar. The three main plans are **Basic ($10/mo)**, **Standard ($30/mo)**, and **Pro ($60/mo)**. Basic gives you about 200 images per month, which is plenty while you're learning. Pick a plan, enter your card details, and confirm.

💬 Example: Choose **Basic Plan → Monthly billing → Confirm payment**.

You'll know it worked when: your account shows an active subscription, and the prompt input box becomes active (no longer greyed out or locked).

## Step 3 — Write your first prompt

On the Midjourney home page, find the text input area — usually labeled with words like **"Imagine"** or **"Describe what you want to create"**. Click inside the box and type a description of the image you want. Keep your first one simple. Then press **Enter** or click **Generate**.

💬 Example prompt to copy:
`a cozy coffee shop at golden hour, watercolor style, soft warm light`

After about 30–60 seconds, you'll see a grid of **four image options** appear below your prompt.

You'll know it worked when: four finished images appear on screen within a minute or two, and no error message shows.

## Step 4 — Pick a favorite and try variations

Below each of the four images, you'll see two rows of buttons: **U1–U4** (upscale that image) and **V1–V4** (create variations of that image). Hover over them to see the full label — usually **Vary (Subtle)** or **Vary (Strong)**. Click **Vary (Subtle)** on whichever image you like best to get four close cousins of it. Try **Vary (Strong)** if you want wilder, more different alternatives.

💬 Example: If image **#2** is your favorite, click **V2 → Vary (Subtle)** to refine it.

You'll know it worked when: a new grid of four refined images appears within a minute, based on the one you picked.

## Step 5 — Upscale your final choice

When you find an image you love, click the matching **U** button (U1–U4). Midjourney processes the image for a few seconds and shows it at full resolution with sharper detail. On the web interface, you can also click the image itself to open a larger preview.

💬 Example: Click **U3** to upscale the third image of your latest grid at full quality.

You'll know it worked when: a single, larger image appears (typically 1024×1024 pixels or more), with no "loading" spinner.

## Step 6 — Save your image

Click your final image to open it in Midjourney's preview window. Look for a **download icon** (usually a small downward arrow) in the top-right corner, or right-click the image and choose **Save image as…**. Save it to your Downloads folder, and you're done.

💬 Example path: `Click image → top-right download arrow → Save as "my-first-midjourney.png"`

You'll know it worked when: the image file appears in your Downloads folder and opens normally on your computer or phone.

## Common mistakes

- **Writing a prompt that's too vague.** "A nice picture" gives you generic results. Add specifics: subject, setting, mood, style. *"A cat on a windowsill at sunset, oil painting style"* beats *"cat picture"* every time.
- **Always picking image #1.** Midjourney's strongest output isn't always the first one. Scan all four results — your favorite is often #2 or #3.
- **Trying to download before upscaling.** Click the **U** button first. Otherwise you'll save a low-resolution thumbnail, not the full-quality image.
- **Pressing Enter with no plan active.** If nothing happens when you submit a prompt, you probably skipped Step 2. Subscribe first, then the prompt box unlocks.

## What this means for you

- **If you create for fun**: Your first prompt should be about something you already love — your pet, your kitchen, your favorite hobby. You'll learn faster when the result matters to you.
- **If you run a small business or side project**: Use Midjourney for blog headers, social posts, and product mockups before paying a designer. It's not a replacement, but it's a fast way to test visual ideas.
- **If you're brand new to AI images**: Stick to the website (midjourney.com) — the Discord version looks chaotic for first-timers. Save your favorite prompts in a notes app; you'll reuse them.

Your next step today: open **midjourney.com**, sign in, and generate one image of something you'd genuinely enjoy — a portrait of your dog, a dream kitchen, a poster for your favorite band. See what comes back.
